OVERVIEW

[
1
]

Upon application of some defendants in U.S. litigation,
the U.S. court agreed to issue a request to the Québec Superior Court for judicial
assistance, asking that it order communication of documents and oral testimony from
a non-party corporation based in Québec.  The non-party is the parent
corporation of the plaintiff which instituted the U.S. litigation against those
defendants.

[
2
]

The U.S. court’s request, in the form of letters
rogatory, sets out the key facts in the dispute, states the subject matter which
serves to identify documents and focus oral testimony, affirms the relevance
and proportionality of the evidence sought and informs that the parties in the
U.S. Litigation have exhausted alternative means of obtaining that evidence.

[
3
]

The non-party parent corporation does not object
to a representative participating as a witness in a rogatory commission but does
object to the scope of the evidence sought. The non-party parent argues that the
rogatory commission seeks irrelevant, vaguely worded evidence whose collection
would constitute a trial of its operations. The non-party also objects to
communicating certain sets of documents it identified as responsive to the
document demands but subject to protections based on public order, privilege
and confidentiality.

[
4
]

Not all the parties in the U.S. litigation participated
in the Québec Superior Court hearing regarding whether to authorize execution
of the rogatory commission.  Those other parties would have access to the
evidence provided by the non-party based in Québec but not be bound by any
resulting order of the Québec Superior Court.

[
5
]

For the reasons set out below, the Court authorizes
in part execution of the rogatory commission, stipulating terms and conditions
for the conduct of the examination and communication of documents. The Court
also determines the objections, denying access altogether for certain documents
and authorizing access to others in redacted form, and reserves jurisdiction to
determine objections based on public order, privilege and confidentiality.

1.

REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE

[
6
]

Rossetti Associates Incorporated and Matthew L.
Rossetti Architect (individually and collectively “
Rossetti
”) are named defendants
in the United States District Court Eastern District of New York file Docket
no. 1:17–cv–00214-RRM-RER

(“
U.S. Litigation
”) instituted
by Canam Steel Corporation (“
Canam Steel
”).

[
7
]

In addition to Rossetti, other entities appear
as named defendants in the U.S. Litigation: Hunt Construction Group, Inc. (“
Hunt
”),
WSP US Corp. (“
WSP
”), USTA National Tennis Center Incorporated (“
USTA
”)
and Derr and Isbell Construction, LLC (“
Derr Isbell
”) (individually and
collectively “
Other U.S. Defendants
”).

[
8
]

The parties to U.S. Litigation dispute their
respective rights and obligations related to the design, development and
construction of a free-standing retractable fabric roof and steel support
structure at the Arthur Ashe Tennis Stadium located in Flushing Meadows, New
York (“
Project
”).

[
9
]

As plaintiff, Canam Steel claims against
Rossetti alleging Rossetti’s negligent misrepresentation and negligence. As
defendant against Canam Steel’s claims, Rossetti not only denies the alleged misrepresentations
and negligence but intends to establish that Canam Steel is responsible for its
own losses for the Project, due to Canam Steel’s own underbidding.

[
10
]

As part of the pre-trial evidentiary phase in
the U.S. Litigation, Rossetti determined that it needed evidence from a non-party
located outside the jurisdiction of the United States District Court Eastern
District of New York (“
N.Y. Court
”). The Québec-based non-party, Canam
Group Inc. (“
Canam Group
”), is the parent company of Canam Steel.

[
11
]

Materials submitted by Rossetti inform that
Canam Group specializes in the installation of structural steel products in the
industrial and commercial sectors. A multi-tiered, complex structure of operations
spread across many jurisdictions and engaged in various types of construction
projects, Canam Group operates twenty-three (23) plants across North America
and employs over 4,300 people. Canam Steel is but one of Canam Group’s
subsidiaries.

[
12
]

Rossetti applied to the N.Y. Court to have it
issue a request for the assistance of Québec judicial authorities to order
Canam Group to provide documents and testimony for use in the U.S. Litigation.
None of the Other U.S. Defendants applied to the N.Y. Court for the rogatory
commission.  Canam Steel disputed the relevance and need for the rogatory
commission.

[
13
]

After having considered submissions from
Rossetti and Canam Steel,  Mr. Justice Ramon E. Reyes Jr., District Judge, (“
Judge
Reyes
”) issue a July 10, 2020
Request for International Judicial
Assistance (Letters Rogatory)
for a rogatory commission (“
Request
”).
Execution of the rogatory commission as sought by Rossetti and set out in the
Request would order a representative of Canam Group (i) to communicate documents
responsive to twenty-eight (28) detailed document demands (“
Document Demands
”)
set out in Exhibit A to the Request and (ii) to attend a pre-trial examination
compliant with a notice for the examination provided as Exhibit B.

1.1

Rossetti’s Application

[
14
]

In the Québec Superior Court, Rossetti filed an
August 11, 2020
Application for Execution of a Rogatory Commission Issued by
the Court of a Foreign State
(“
Application
”) under
article 504
of
Québec’s

Code of Civil Procedure, CQLR c C-25.01
(“
C.C.P.
”). The
Application asks that the Québec Superior Court authorize execution of the
rogatory commission as set out in the Request.

[
15
]

The Application provides meaningful insight into
the U.S. Litigation, including the key facts of the dispute.  The Application
proposes the subject matter of the document demands and oral testimony, the procedure
to conduct the document communication and examination, including a full list of
individuals to notify for attendance at the examination, and express provision
that a videographer attend to record the testimony.

[
16
]

The Application informs that the oral evidence and
documents are intended for use in the U.S. Litigation and may be used at trial.
None of the Other U.S. Defendants or Canam Steel participated in any of the exchanges
with the Québec Superior Court regarding the Application or attended the
hearings. Rossetti and Canam Group confirm that, despite their absence, the
Other U.S. Defendants and Canam Steel will have equal access to evidence communicated
by Rossetti should the Application be authorized.

1.2

Preliminary Determination - October 12 and 13, 2021 hearing

[
17
]

Further to an earlier attendance, the parties were
scheduled to proceed on October 12 and 13, 2021 to debate the Application. Assigned
to hear the Application, the Court requested that Rossetti and Canam Group
participate in a case management hearing.

[
18
]

At the October 7, 2021 case management hearing,
Canam Group advised that it did not object
per se
to the Court
authorizing execution of a rogatory commission.  Rather, Canam Group reserved
its submissions, as did Rossetti, on the scope and conduct of any rogatory
commission, if and when authorized.

[
19
]

Rather than use the October dates as a hearing
on the merits of the Application, both Rossetti and Canam Group raised a
preliminary issue which they jointly asked the Court to resolve in advance of a
hearing on the merits of the Application. The preliminary issue arose because the
Request required that documents responsive to the Document Demands be
communicated to Rossetti’s Québec counsel twenty (20) days in advance of the
examination.

[
20
]

Asking that documents be communicated before
questioning the witness at an oral examination is a perfectly rationale sequence.
If reflects reasonable, if not best, practices in using the time and resources
of those engaged in an examination.  That sequence, however, failed to
accommodate for a particular statute of public order in force in Québec, the
Business
Concerns Records Act, CQLR c D-12
(“
BCRA
”). Rossetti and Canam Group
both requested that the original October 12, and 13, 2021 hearing concern the
preliminary determination of Rossetti’s access, if any, to documents subject to
the BCRA.  The Court agreed.

[
21
]

The day after the case management hearing, Canam
Group communicated to the Court a collection of two hundred and eighty-three
(283) documents (“
Initial Document Set
”) and the October 7, 2021
affidavit Mtre. Frédéric Gendron, attorney.

[
22
]

Collected following service of the Application,
the Initial Document Set reflected Canam Group’s initial determination of those
documents responsive to the Document Demands. The Initial Document Set comprised
Canam Group’s without prejudice, initial-efforts response to the Document
Demands.  Canam Group informed that its response was limited by what it
asserted were vague descriptions of the documents sought. Canam Group cautioned
that its ability to provide the Initial Document Set did not constitute a
concession that the Document Demands sufficiently described relevant
documents.  Canam Group therefore advised that other documents could still be
sourced.

[
23
]

Canam Group organized the Initial Document Set
as follows into five (5) sets of binders:

Binder A, volumes 1 and 2 - one
hundred and ninety-eight (198) documents subject to the
BCRA
(“
BCRA
Documents
”)

Binder B - ten (10) documents subject
to litigation privilege (“
Litigation Privilege Documents
”)

Binder C - two (2) documents subject
to solicitor-client privilege (“
Solicitor-Client Privilege Documents
”)

Binder D and Binder E - respectively
six (6) documents and sixty-seven (67) documents not subject to
BCRA
but
subject to a confidentiality interest and which Canam Group sought to withhold
or, in the alternative, provide only in redacted form (“
Confidential
Documents
”)

[
24
]

Canam Group provided the Court with a copy of the
entire contents of Binders A, B and C. Canam Group provided the entire contents
Binders D and E in two (2) versions: a full version and a version redacted for
confidentiality.

[
25
]

Rosetti received notice of communication to the
Court of the binders but no copy of Binders A, B and C and a copy of the full
and redacted versions of Binders D and E. Canam Group provided Rossetti with indexes
of the documents, other than BCRA Documents, and the Court would need not specify
the contents of those binders other than by the letters of the binders.

[
26
]

The parties devoted October 12, and 13, 2021 (“
October
BCRA Hearing
”) to the preliminary determination of Rossetti’s
access, if any, to the BCRA Documents in Binder A, volumes 1 and 2.  After
hearing the parties, the Court issued its decision orally on October 13, 2021, (“
BCRA
Decision
”).
[1]

In the BCRA Decision, the Court acknowledged that the Request specifically asked
that Canam Group be ordered to communicate relevant documents first, then provide
a representative to participate in the oral examination. The Court observed that
the sequence was reasonable but difficult to reconcile with the role the
BCRA

plays in restricting communication of documents subject to its provisions.

[
27
]

The Court held that determination of access to
the
BCRA
was premature on the facts available.  The Court modified the Request’s
sequence.  The Court required that the oral examination proceed before document
demands concerning the BCRA Documents, on terms and conditions stipulated in
the BCRA Decision. Though not ideal, reversing the sequence preserved the
capacity of the Québec Superior Court to offer its assistance
[2]
without violating the BCRA.

[
28
]

The modified sequence provided Rossetti, the
Other U.S. Defendants, Canam Steel and Canam Group the opportunity to establish
sufficient facts relevant to the
BCRA
’s application to documents responsive to a
rogatory commission as authorized by a subsequent decision on the merits of the
Application.
[3]

QUESTIONS IN ISSUE

[
29
]

The BCRA Decision did not deal with the
documents in Binder B, Binder C, Binder D and Binder E or any of Canam Group’s
objections in regard to the Litigation Privilege Documents, Solicitor-Client
Privilege Documents and Confidential Documents (“
Objections
”). As agreed, the parties attended a second hearing on November 25
and 26, 2021 (“
November Application Hearing
”) for the purpose of
adjudicating the Application and the objections raised by Canam Group.  Each of
the parties communicated additional materials for the record.

[
30
]

Given the contents of the Application, the Request
and Canam Group’s Objections and the record constituted for the November Application
Hearing, the Court identified certain questions. Should the Court:

(i) grant Rossetti’s Application
and authorize execution of the rogatory commission as sought by the Request, for
collection and use of the evidence in the U.S. Litigation, in whole or in part?
If granted, on what terms and conditions?

(ii)(a) maintain Canam Group’s
objections regarding (a) Solicitor-Client Privilege Documents for collection
and use of the evidence in the U.S. Litigation? If maintained only in part, on
what terms and conditions?

(ii)(b) maintain Cana m Group’s
objections regarding Litigation Privilege Documents for collection and use of
the evidence in the U.S. Litigation? If maintained only in part, on what terms
and conditions?

(ii)(c) maintain Canam Group’s
objections regarding Confidential Documents for collection and use of the
evidence in the U.S. Litigation? If maintained only in part, on what terms and
conditions?

[
31
]

For the reasons which follow, based on the
record, the submissions of Rossetti and Canam Group, the applicable principles,
interests and criteria established by legislation and case law, the Court:

(i) grants Rosetti’s Application in
part, to execute the rogatory commission for collection and use of the evidence
in the U.S. Litigation by Rossetti, the Other U.S. Defendants and Canam Steel, according
to certain terms and conditions;

(ii)(a) determines that each of the
Solicitor-Client Privilege Documents qualifies for the stated privilege and maintains
Canam Group’s objections to communicate those documents;

(ii)(b) determines that each of the
Litigation Privilege Documents qualifies for the stated privilege and maintains
Canam Group’s objections to communicate those documents; and,

(ii)(c) determines that each of the
Confidential Documents qualifies as confidential but, being relevant, maintains
only in part the objections and orders communication of them in their redacted
versions for use in the U.S. Litigation to Rossetti, the Other U.S. Defendants
and Canam Steel, according to certain terms and conditions.

Approach

[
32
]

The Court will address the Application first and
then the Objections.  For the Application, the Court will first identify the
key principles and interests which motivate judicial assistance and govern the
exercise of judicial discretion when deciding whether to authorize execution of
a rogatory commission.  The Court next notes the discretion Québec courts have
in offering the assistance and then lists the criteria developed by the case
law against which the elements of a rogatory commission are measured.

[
33
]

The Court will clarify the status of Canam Group
to the U.S. Litigation and then apply the principles, discretion and criteria
to the elements requested in the rogatory commission.  In doing so, the Court
will set out the scope of the subject matter and demands for documents sought
by Rossetti and then determine the authorized subject matter and authorized
document demands. The Court will close by stipulating further terms and
conditions.

[
34
]

For the Objections, the Court will address and
determine first the Solicitor-Client Privilege, next the Litigation Privilege and
then the Confidential Documents and, where needed, set out terms and conditions.

APPLICABLE
PRINCIPLES

[
35
]

Article 504
-
506

C.C.P.
comprise Québec’s provisions
on execution of rogatory commissions issued in a foreign state. They follow

articles 499
-
503
C.C.P. which govern rogatory commissions issued in Québec. Despite
being informed by those which precede them, articles 504 C.C.P.
et seq.
offer
the courts little insight into how Québec courts ought to authorize execution
of the rogatory commissions.

[
36
]

Instead, case law has identified the key principles,
interests and criteria which assist Québec courts when deciding whether to
authorize execution of rogatory commissions. Those principles, interests and
criteria originate from Z
ingre v. The Queen et al.,
1981 CanLII 32 (SCC)
,

[1981] 2 SCR 392
(“
Zingre
”). Released over forty (40) years ago,
Zingre

continues to guide Québec courts.

[
37
]

Zingre
held that Canada’s
international legal assistance rests on the principle of comity of nations. Comity
motivates one jurisdiction’s courts to assist another jurisdiction’s courts by
giving effect to the latter jurisdiction’s laws and judicial decisions.  Comity
urges the first jurisdiction to do so out of mutual deference and respect to
the other but also because of convenience, necessity and common interest.
[4]
Canadians participate in an
integrated world economy governed by a diversity of autonomous legal systems. Canadians
share a common interest with others to accommodate the back-and-forth flows of
wealth, skills and people across jurisdictions. With those flows come disputes
and with those disputes comes a need to participate in solving them.

[
38
]

The Request reflects the similar comity, closing
with the following:

IX Reciprocity
- The Courts for the United States are authorized by statute, Section 1782,
Title 28 of the United States Code, to extend similar assistance to foreign
courts.  The United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York
would be willing to provides similar assistance to the Courts of Canada.

[
39
]

Execution of a rogatory commission is neither an
absolute obligation nor mere courtesy and goodwill.
[5]
Execution involves an exercise
of discretion but one that is not untethered.
[6]

That discretion, “
like all judicial discretion, must be exercised
judiciously, meaning that it must be based on legal rules and principles
”.
[7]

[
40
]

Courts across Canada have drawn on
Zingre

to develop those rules and principles which tether their discretion. Despite different
procedural matrices, the courts have developed a shared approach to such
requests.
[8]

Québec courts often refer to Ontario case law.
[9]

Both Rossetti and Canam Group provided written submissions and case law which
disclosed the Québec courts’ references to reasoning applied in Ontario
regarding rogatory commissions.
[10]

Though not bound by that reasoning, Québec courts have endorsed it as persuasive.
[11]
As recent illustration,
United
States Securities and Exchange Commission v. Ouellet,
2018 QCCS 4239
expressly
referenced criteria set out in
Aker Biomarine AS
et al. v. KGK Synergize
Inc.,
2013 ONSC 4897
.
[12]

[
41
]

The case law discloses that the principle of comity
alone does not inform the courts’ exercise of discretion. The courts must also consider
the interests in respecting the public policy of the jurisdiction to which the
request is directed and in ensuring absence of prejudice to the sovereignty or
the witnesses of that jurisdiction.
[13]

Regarding the interests of public policy and absence of prejudice, the courts
assess whether execution of a particular rogatory commission would: (i) violate
relevant Canadian or provincial law; (ii) infringe on recognized Canadian moral
or legal principles; (iii) impose an undue burden on the witness of whom the
request is made; or (iv) do prejudice to that witness.
[14]

[
42
]

Despite use of the term “
balancing
” in
the case law, the principle of comity is the lightest when weighed against the
interests. If the rogatory commission respects public policy and creates no
prejudice, then comity justifies granting the assistance. A court’s assistance is therefore much more
than a rubberstamp
[15]

and involves the courts’ scrutiny of the impact of the execution of a rogatory
commission.The Québec court must consider the impact on the witness and
not submit the witness to more duties or less protection that what the courts
would impose on witnesses in Québec courts.
[16]

[
43
]

As set out below, the case law has developed criteria in
compliance with
Zingre
and the consideration of the principle of comity
and the interests of public policy and absence of prejudice. Before listing the
criteria applicable to its analysis, the Court will first identify the discretion
Québec courts have to tailor elements of a rogatory commission if and when an
element fails to comply with the criteria.  Québec courts use their discretion
to ensure that they can offer assistance which, though not identical to the
initial request, remains meaningful for the purpose of the foreign dispute
resolution.

2.

DISCRETION

[
44
]

A rogatory commission may include elements
which, if executed, would violate some of the criteria identified by the case
law.  The Québec court need not just reject the foreign court’s request for
assistance.  Comity expects more.  Within their jurisdiction to offer judicial
assistance, Québec courts have discretion to authorize less than what is sought
as well as to impose terms and conditions.

[
45
]

Discretion presumes jurisdiction. To offer
assistance which remains meaningful to foreign courts and compliant with the
criteria, Québec courts have the following discretion:

(i) authorize
less assistance than requested

(ii) respond
to whether foreign court provides familiar procedure

(iii) make
or revisit determinations

(iv) apply standard
of relevance where evidence collected

(v) accept
evidence of context

(vi) reduce
disputes post-authorization

(vii) impose
terms and conditions regarding access to and use of evidence

(viii) retain
jurisdiction to safeguard public order and privilege

2.1

Authorize less assistance than requested

[
46
]

Less is better than none. Québec’s C.C.P. reflects
no legislative imperative obliging Québec courts to approach execution as an
all or nothing.
[17]

The process is not some form of final offer arbitration in which the Québec court
can only opt between either of the competing positions to accept or reject, without
an option somewhere between the opposites.
[18]

In Ontario, the courts “
may narrow their orders accordingly
”
[19]
and so can the Québec courts.
[20]

[
47
]

A flexible approach complies with the
C.C.P.

The C.C.P. is designed to provide means to prevent and resolve disputes, to avoid
litigation through appropriate, efficient and fair-minded processes, to ensure fair,
simple, proportionate and economical application of its procedural rules and to
respect those involved in the administration of justice.
[21]
Those involved in the
administration of justice involve non-parties, such as Canam Group, called upon
to participate as witnesses and litigants before foreign courts, such as
Rossetti, authorized by those courts to seek relevant assistance for the
purpose of their foreign dispute resolution.

[
48
]

The
C.C.P.
expressly mentions that the Québec courts
are also held to observe the same guiding principles of proportionality when
issuing orders and authorizing measures and acts. The C.C.P. requires that Québec
courts ensure that their orders or authorizations comply with the proportionality
principles, while having regard to the proper administration of justice.
[22]
One such authorized measure and
act is the execution of a rogatory commission under
article 504
C.C.P. A judicious
consideration of comity and the interests identified in
Zingre
and the
criteria developed by subsequent case law includes reliance on principles of
proportionality to inform the decision making.

[
49
]

The criteria are more than useful
guideposts. Each criterion is necessary. Failure to respect any single
criterion can, in and of itself, justify a refusal to authorize execution. If offering less assistance than requested allows the Québec court
to offer some assistance, then the court ought to trim down on the request. Offering
less allows the Québec courts to comply with public order and avoid prejudice
to the sovereignty or the witnesses and still respond to comity.

2.2

Respond to whether foreign provides familiar procedure

[
50
]

Differences in discovery may exist between the
Québec court and the foreign court regarding the collection of evidence and its
subsequent use in the foreign court and by the parties gaining access to it. The
greater the parallel between the Québec court’s procedure and that of the foreign
court, the easier for the Québec court to determine whether execution of the
rogatory commission complies with Canadian standards. Awareness of such
differences, if any, informs a Québec court’s appreciation of the foreign
court’s own adjudication of the initial request to issue letters rogatory.

[
51
]

In the present case, the letters rogatory issue
from the U.S.   Canadian courts have commented that Canada and the U.S. might have
comparable legal systems but their respective rules for pre-trial examinations
or discovery are “
significantly dissimilar
”.
[23]
In relative terms, U.S. jurisdictions
have been styled as having “
vastly more permissive rules governing discovery
”.
[24]

[
52
]

Certain Canadian decisions have observed that
discovery from non-parties is the norm in U.S. civil litigation, available without
need for a prior order of the court to examine a non-party or to compel a
non-party to produce documents.
[25]

In Québec, as in Ontario, examination of a non-party and production of
documents is the exception rather than the rule.
[26]

[
53
]

Québec courts are alert to but not critical of
such differences. Being alert to the more permissive discovery rules in the
U.S. prompts Québec courts to examine whether the letters rogatory might have
issued: (i) in a perfunctory manner or without a suitable hearing; (ii) without
considerations familiar in Québec courts of the impact of the request; (iii)
without testing the evidence relied on in support of the request; and, (iv)
without notice to or input from the non-party.
[27]

[
54
]

While Québec courts extend their assistance,
they do so mindful of the standards applicable within their jurisdiction. Québec
courts evaluate whether the foreign court offers similar safeguards regarding subsequent
use of the evidence to be given.  One such safeguard in Québec is the implied
undertaking of confidentiality.
[28]

A witness ordered to participate in a rogatory commission does not leave the Québec
jurisdiction.  The witness never leaves the jurisdiction, only the evidence
given. The foreign court effectively visits the jurisdiction and abides by the
rules inherent in the system here. A witness, ordered to participate, retains
all his or her rights, including protections accepted in Québec as inherent or
implicit in the civil judicial process.  When in Canada, do as the Canadians
do.

[
55
]

In Québec civil procedure, evidence given by a witness
merits different protections.  Those protections preserve the privacy interest invested
in the evidence by the witness, the confidentiality interest attached to the information
shared and its impact on the witness’ activities, both personal and
commercial.  An important interest recognized in Québec civil procedure is that
any evidence given will be used in the dispute for which it is communicated and
will not serve as a trampoline to further disputes, involving the witness or
not, based on what is revealed in the evidence.

[
56
]

As a result, even where a rogatory commission
does not so provide, the Québec courts can include in its order terms and
conditions which duplicate or reflect the protections which apply in Québec to
witnesses and the evidence collected.

This
conclusion may seem unusual to jurists accustomed to a different system of
litigation. But this court must exercise its jurisdiction and its discretionary
power in a way that will not subject Quebec citizens to an ordeal that is not
compatible, in this specific situation, with our rules and our legal system.
[29]

[
57
]

Québec courts also evaluate whether the request
will submit the witness to the procedural elements familiar to the foreign
court but considered unusual or unnecessary here. Videotaping testimony may be
common practice in the foreign court but the same is not true in Québec courts.
Québec courts are not bound to include those procedural elements or justify
why such elements are not included.  Québec courts are open to be persuaded to
add new elements to a witness’ experience but are not obliged to impose them on
the witness who does not leave the jurisdiction.

2.3

Make or revisit determinations

[
58
]

Authorizing execution of a rogatory commission
has been likened to a request to examine a third party under
article 221

C.C.P.
[30]
The court’s order effectively
authorizes the issuance of a subpoena except that the subpoena issues at the
request of a foreign court and for its purposes.
[31]
Because execution of a
rogatory commission orders a witness to participate in an examination and to communicate
documents, some qualify the impact on the witness as an injunction.
[32]

[
59
]

Unless there was a requirement to have served
the witness with the initial application in the foreign court,
[33]
the witness will not have
had any meaningful input into the process which led to the letters rogatory
being issued. The witness is entitled to be heard in the Québec court when an
application is presented to execute the rogatory commission. The witness, now a
party to that application, can contest by presenting argument and adducing additional
evidence to the record.
[34]

[
60
]

The Québec court ought therefore to expect that
aspects of the rogatory commission will be re-argued once the witness is
involved.  Allowing this debate is not a lack of deference to the foreign court
but merely respect for
audi alterum partem
for the witness.

2.4

Apply standard of relevance where evidence collected

[
61
]

The criteria identified below require, among
other things, that the evidence sought be relevant. A Québec court does not limit
its analysis of relevance to a display of deference to determinations asserted
on relevance or to the standard applied by the foreign court. To do so would
allow deference to suppress jurisdiction. While the rogatory commission may have
met the foreign court’s standard for relevance, the rogatory commission must
also meet the Québec court’s own standards. In other words, the evidence must
meet the standard set by the foreign court and the standard set by the Québec
court.  Deference is given to the first but jurisdiction requires the Québec
court’s own analysis in the second.

[
62
]

For both steps of relevance, the court must
determine the issues in the foreign litigation.

[
63
]

In Québec, courts analyse relevance principally
in regard to the allegations in the pleadings and exhibits.
[35]
Doing so makes sense when
civil procedure drafting standards oblige parties to plead in a detailed
manner.  Not all courts have the same approach. Québec’s approach may misjudge
relevance if the foreign court, like certain jurisdictions, relied on summary
or notice pleadings compliant with their civil procedure. Québec’s approach may
skew conclusions if the Québec court considers that the allegations in the
foreign court’s procedures lack the detail expected here.

[
64
]

The Québec court ought to adjust its analysis of
relevance to accommodate relevant differences, if any, between its civil
procedure and that of the foreign court’s. The Québec court must anticipate
whether the foreign court’s own rules of procedure require less detailed
pleadings than here.

[
65
]

In such cases, the parties to the application
for execution should demonstrate whether, in addition to summary or notice
style pleadings, the parties in the foreign court filed and relied on letters
or other interim pleadings when seeking and resisting the rogatory commission.
Those materials are necessarily material to relevance and ought to be permitted
to form part of the record for the exercise of discretion.

[
66
]

If not already included in the letters rogatory,
the court must set out the subject matter authorized for the examination and
communication of documents.

2.5

Accept evidence of context

[
67
]

The court cannot exercise its discretion in a
factual  vacuum.
[36]

Affirmations in the letters rogatory are not determinative for the Québec court.
An application to execute the rogatory commission must provide sufficient
context and the witness is entitled to submit evidence which does not appear in
the letters rogatory or the application for execution.
[37]

[
68
]

Such evidence involves not just the substance of
the dispute before the foreign court but the nature of the hearing in the foreign
court which led to issuance of the letters rogatory. The Québec court’s goal is
not to redo what has been done already by the foreign court but provide the Québec
court a clear idea of the foreign court’s prior look at relevance.  This
evidence allows the court to give deference to the process in the foreign court
once it understands what the process was.

[
69
]

Evidence might demonstrate the nature of the hearing
and include any written materials or exhibits provided for the foreign court’s
initial determination. The judge who issued the request may have had extensive,
prior case management duties.  Such involvement can reassure that the initial
decision was fully informed given the issues raised in the foreign court. The
evidence can also inform whether the request issued after a full hearing or
only from a summary or documents-only hearing.

2.6

Reduce post-authorization disputes

[
70
]

At its heart, the assistance serves to enable
dispute resolution in a foreign jurisdiction. Designed to resolve a dispute,
the assistance ought not to give life to new disputes.

[
71
]

Québec courts can add terms and conditions which
focus on the mechanics of the examination and communication of documents in
order to avoid creating future misunderstandings. The court is not limited by
the mechanics sought or omitted in the request issued by the foreign court.

[
72
]

Adding terms and conditions for that purpose
differs from granting more than was requested.  As already noted, Québec courts
can trim down on requests to offer assistance but, absent consent of those
involved including the parties to the foreign litigation and the witness, the
Québec court cannot order the collection of more evidence than what the foreign
court requested. The application for execution of rogatory commission, and any
order on that application, must fall within the foreign court’s request. Any
overreach in the requesting party’s application is ignored.

[
73
]

First, the Québec court can speak to the
duration of the examination,  confirm authorization that non-Canadian attorneys
be expressly authorized to attend or conduct the examination, and provide for translation
services. The court can provide that the witness be accompanied by an attorney.
[38]
The attorney’s role is
limited to the role assigned by the local procedure with any acceptable
modifications made on consent or by the foreign court’s own procedures not in
conflict with Canadian laws.

[
74
]

Second, in the new era introduced by
technological responses to COVID, the Québec court ought to ensure comparable
access to technology to keep the witness on a level playing field.  It is not
suitable to have a witness have only one screen if the parties will necessarily
present documents on a share screen thereby interfering with witness’ virtual
participation. If the record discloses the concerns, the court can address
them.

[
75
]

Third, the Québec court can also order that the
witness obtain a full, free copy of the stenographer’s notes and exhibits
spoken to by the witness, subject to any conditions necessary to ensure the
confidentiality of the contents. If a record of the testimony is important
enough to record for the parties seeking it, the same record is important
enough for the witness giving it.

[
76
]

Fourth, the Québec court can provide that the
process be conducted under specific rules of procedure. A party seeking such
specificity ought to provide excerpts of such rules and include affidavit from
a member of the foreign bar if those rules are disputed. The evidence serves to
complete the Québec court’s understanding of what it is asked to authorize.
Without such evidence, the Québec court could elect to refrain from imposing
rules of procedure it has not considered.  Doing so is not advisable as it
leaves the potential for future disagreements between the parties and the
witness.

2.7

Impose terms and conditions to access and use evidence

[
77
]

Québec courts can add terms and conditions which
address concerns raised during the court’s analysis on the criteria. Such terms
and conditions serve to avoid placing the witness in potential breach of his or
her obligations or compromising the witness’ rights. Such orders might impose a
confidentiality order on the evidence or the equivalent of an undertaking not
to use the evidence for any purpose other than in the foreign court.  The
Québec court might recognize and enforce a party’s undertaking to apply for
confidentiality in the foreign court.  The court, however, has no control over
whether that application will be granted or not.

[
78
]

Orders on applications to execute rogatory
commissions will issue against the parties and the witness who appear in the
Québec courts to debate the application. Not all those named as parties to the
foreign court litigation will be named as a party to the application to the
Québec court.  As a result, certain parties in the foreign court litigation
will not be bound by the terms and conditions of the Québec court order but
will still have access to the evidence authorized.

[
79
]

To address their absence from the Québec court
order and their access to the evidence, the Québec courts have jurisdiction to
impose conditions precedent on communication of or access to the oral and
documentary evidence.  Such conditions may require that all recipients of the
evidence be bound by the terms of the Québec court order.  The order can
provide that the parties consent to the terms in order to access the evidence
or that the foreign court can issue a suitable order in lieu of consent. The
conditions precedent need not be realized but then the evidence need not be communicated.
A Québec court is not obliged to offer assistance but has an interest in offering
what is permitted.  In similar manner, a foreign court is not obliged to accept
the assistance offered but has an interest in accepting what is permitted.

[
80
]

As noted above, the Request closed with its own
confirmation of reciprocity, including the “
United
States District Court for the Eastern District of New York would be willing to
provides similar assistance to the Courts of Canada”
. The Court understands that the reciprocity mentioned speaks mainly
to affirm comity.  The Court also anticipates that the said reciprocity must
also be interpreted as willingness to impose terms and conditions attached to a
Canadian court’s assistance given in response to such an request from the same U.S.
court.

2.8

Retain jurisdiction to safeguard public order and privileges

[
81
]

In Québec, a witness cannot refuse to answer a
question on the basis of relevance.
[39]

For that reason, the court authorizing execution of  the rogatory commission can
defer the right to raise such objections during the examination.
[40]

When authorizing execution of the rogatory commission, Québec courts may order
that the examination and communication of documents be conducted in the manner
in which the foreign court determines objections, if any, regarding relevance.
This deferral ought to be done only in tandem to Québec courts stipulating the authorized
scope of relevant subject matter. Québec courts still reserve discretion to
limit the witness’ obligation to respond if circumstances justify doing so.
[41]

[
82
]

Dealing with objections in advance may be
premature but the witness is not precluded from contesting the validity in
advance of the examination and any communication of documents.
[42]

[
83
]

Québec courts do retain jurisdiction to resolve
objections based on public policy, public order and privilege. Objections
include those based on the duty of discretion of public servants, professional
secrecy, the protection of the confidentiality of a journalistic source, as
well as fundamental rights or evidence which raise a substantial and legitimate
interest.
[43]

In such cases, under Québec law, the witness may refrain from answering.

[
84
]

In its order, the court may stipulate to such
objections if the record provides reasonable foreseeability that they may
arise. Retaining jurisdiction on such matters can be stipulated in the formal
order.  Omission to do so in the order, in whole or in part, cannot be treated
as a denial of the witness’ rights to raise them to the Québec Superior Court
if they do arise subsequent to the execution of the rogatory commission.

3.

CRITERIA

[
85
]

With the above discretion in mind, the Court now
turns to the criteria developed by the case law.

[
86
]

The list is cumulative. An order authorizing
execution of the rogatory commission must comply with each of the criteria. If
execution conflicts with any one of the criteria and none of the tools can
resolve that conflict, comity cedes its place.
[44]

As set out in the preceding section, the Québec courts have the tools of
discretion to trim requests which do not meet the criteria and to add terms and
conditions to reduce post-authorization disputes and address concerns raised by
the criteria.  The following are those criteria:

(i) not
contrary to Canadian jurisdiction’s public policy or public order

(ii) oral testimony
and/or communication of documents

(iii) relevant
to issues measured by Canadian jurisdiction’s standards

(iv) reasonable
specificity, compliant with Canadian jurisdiction’s principles

(v) use of
the evidence for pre-trial and/or trial

(vi) not
otherwise obtainable or unduly burdensome

3.1

Not contrary to Canadian jurisdiction’s public policy or public
order

[
87
]

The rogatory commission must not be contrary to public
policy or public order in the Canadian jurisdiction. The
list of criteria includes express mention of “
public policy
” but the
case law includes consideration of “
public order
”, including those
established by legislation or recognized by the courts. Not every jurisdiction
has the same rules of public order.  Only Ontario with its
Business Records
Protection Act, RSO 1990, c B.19
establishes rules of public order
equivalent to Québec’s
BCRA
.

[
88
]

First, a Québec court’s order granting the
request must comply with limits established by legislation and recognized by courts
for privilege.  Such privileges include solicitor-client, litigation brief
privilege, settlement privilege and mediation privilege.  Non-compellability of
certain participants such as lawyers and mediators continue to apply.

[
89
]

The potential for breach is not a reason to
dismiss the application for execution.  Rather, as noted, the Québec court can require
that the foreign court impose measures similar to those established in
jurisdiction for confidentiality and implied undertaking and do so as a
condition precedent to communicating the documents outside of the jurisdiction.

[
90
]

Second, the Québec court is entitled to presume that
the foreign court’s request respects public policy and public order applicable in
the foreign jurisdiction. The presumption is rebuttable. Potential breaches ought
to be brought to the Québec court’s attention or be noted on its own
initiative. The court can anticipate whether its order might oblige the witness
here to give evidence which might breach foreign laws.

[
91
]

Ordering a witness here to give personal
information on employees in the foreign jurisdiction may breach privacy
obligations in the jurisdiction. The court may include terms and conditions
which defer that determination to the presiding judge to authorize such
communication rather than simply order the response a being relevant
information.

[
92
]

The Québec courts retain jurisdiction to respond
to material evidence that, if granted as sought, might result in a witness
breaching such order or policy in the foreign jurisdiction.
[45]

3.2

Oral testimony and/or communication of documents

[
93
]

For pre-trial evidence used within a particular
jurisdiction, some Canadian civil procedure rules might only expressly
authorize a non-party’s pre-trial involvement to communicating documents while
others might expressly authorize a non-party’s pre-trial examination.
[46]

[
94
]

A rogatory commission may seek a non-party’s attendance
as witness to give oral testimony, communication of documents or both and may
also propose a sequence. A party applying for execution of a rogatory
commission can seek to have communication of documents before deciding whether
to proceed to oral examination.
[47]

The Québec courts can authorize both oral testimony and documents or only one
form of evidence and do so in stages if it is satisfied that circumstances
warrant doing so.

[
95
]

When authorizing the oral examination and
communication of documents as part of a rogatory commission, Québec courts
ought to anticipate if the foreign jurisdiction imposes any limits on the use
of the evidence at trial.  Such rules might require either a new order
authorizing same or express authorization.  To pre-empt a second application or
confusion, the Québec court can expressly authorize use of the evidence at
trial, subject to the rules in the foreign court or authorization of the
foreign court. As noted below, Rossetti addressed this issue in its evidence
and in its draft order.

[
96
]

As indicated in the earlier BCRA Decision,
considerations of public order may require going against a sequence sought by
the letters rogatory even when the Québec courts would recognize that sequence as
best practices.  While not ideal, adjustments allow the foreign dispute
resolution to proceed with appropriate assistance.

3.3

Relevant to issues measured by Canadian jurisdiction’s standards

[
97
]

The evidence sought by the letters rogatory must
be relevant to issues raised in the foreign dispute resolution. Relevance must
be evaluated by standards applicable in the foreign court and by measure of the
standards applicable in the Québec court.

[
98
]

Québec courts are reluctant to exercise their
discretion in a factual void.
[48]

Though the letters rogatory itself may be considered a sufficient evidentiary basis
for an application to execute the letters, the applicant seeking execution must
provide sufficient evidence of the context in which the Québec court is asked
to exercise its discretion.

[
99
]

The Québec courts do not stop at whether the
testimony and documents qualify as relevant within the standards applied in the
foreign court. That is a minimum. If the evidence is not relevant there, the
enquiry terminates and the request ought to be denied.  The Québec courts must
apply their own standard of relevance as part of the exercise of their
discretion.

[
100
]

Parties must state the standard applicable in the foreign court and
adduce a record sufficient for the Québec court to determine how the foreign
court determined relevance before issuing the request.  Relevance is measured
against (i) the pleadings filed in the foreign court as well as material
information submitted in the foreign court, including submissions, interim
motions, affidavits and exhibits, which contribute to identifying the issues in
dispute and (ii) the admissible materials submitted to the Québec court for the
purpose of the hearing.

[
101
]

Parties and the witness can offer to prove or agree on the
applicable standard of relevance in the foreign court so that they can assist
the Québec court in determining relevance.  This may require only a statement
of the test and reliable sources for it. Its application may require a
jurisconsult

if unusual.  The U.S. standard ought not to require a
juriconsult
but
the standard must be read against the more liberal rules governing discovery.
The same standard might give different results in the U.S. and in Canada.

[
102
]

The courts rely not only on the letters rogatory but also accept
evidence provided in support of applicant’s motion and knowledge acquired by the
court on the documents filed before it for the hearing.
[49]

[
103
]

As noted above, when authorizing the execution of the rogatory
commission, the Québec court ought to stipulate, in the conclusions to its decision,
the express scope of the subject matter on which the witness is required to
testify and to communicate documents. This scope may be absent from or
imperfectly stated in the request. The Québec court has jurisdiction to stipulate
what subject matter is authorized and reduce disagreements over relevance going
forward.

3.4

Reasonable specificity, compliant with Canadian jurisdiction’s
principles

[
104
]

The authorized scope of relevant evidence must be identified with
reasonable specificity compliant with the Québec court’s standards by (i)
clearly delineating the issues on which the witness will testify and (ii)
describing the documents/document sets with reasonable specificity. Providing
for both (i) and (ii) reduces post-authorization disputes over whether the
evidence qualifies as responsive or invasive. Documents can be identified by
category of document and still respect specificity.
[50]

[
105
]

The Québec court order creates obligations and the parties subject
to it are required to conduct themselves in good faith both at the time the
obligation arises and at the time it is performed or extinguished.
[51]
The parties and the witness are
bound to exercise their respective civil rights in accordance with the
requirements of good faith and their good faith is presumed but is rebuttable.
[52]

[
106
]

Asking for “
any and all document
s” may be acceptable provided
that the text which follows that phrase in the document demands is reasonably clear
(i) to the witness making good faith efforts to collect responsive documents and
(ii) to the parties in the foreign court litigation making good faith efforts to
accept the documents as responsive.

3.5

Use of the evidence for pre-trial and/or trial

[
107
]

Certain civil procedure rules restrict use of pre-trial examinations
obtained from non-party witnesses.  Those rules provide that the evidence
obtained cannot be used at trial.  Though not express, that limitation applies
only to use at the trial in the jurisdiction which authorized that pre-trial
examination.
[53]

For rogatory commissions, there are no rules against making such an order in
relation to pre-trial proceedings.
[54]

The case law contains frequent mention that the evidence sought must be “
necessary
for trial
” but the courts can authorize execution of a rogatory commission
even if the evidence will not necessarily form part of the evidence at the
trial on the merits.
[55]

[
108
]

While some courts have proposed that a higher standard be overcome
to execute the rogatory commission directed to pre-trial discovery as opposed
to evidence for trial,
[56]

the courts evaluate, on a case-by-case basis, the role played by “
necessary
”.
The nature of the foreign dispute resolution and the materiality of the
evidence sought together inform what is “
necessary
”.

3.6

Not otherwise obtainable or unduly burdensome

[
109
]

Evidence of the same value as that sought by the rogatory commission
must not otherwise be obtainable from a party in the foreign court or from a
non-party better placed in regard to the facts covered by the request.
[57]
This requirement is not
unusual. It mirrors some Canadian civil procedure rules which expressly state
such requirements as pre-conditions to access non-parties for hearings in their
own jurisdiction.
[58]

[
110
]

The order must also respect local standards for examining
non-parties and not be unduly burdensome for the non-party witness measured
according to the procedural practice in place for the Québec court.

[59]
The courts consider the
proportionality of the requested oral examination and document communication.
[60]
As noted earlier, stipulating
the scope of such examinations serves not only to avoid disagreements but avoid
undue burdens on non-parties.

[
111
]

Compliance with requests to provide testimony and documents can be a
fastidious burden but the test is not whether compliance imposes a burden but
whether that burden is undue.
[61]

Observing that the “
purpose of the justice system is to enable the parties
to make their proof by not unduly infringing on the rights of third parties
”,
[62]
the courts have sought to
limit but not eliminate such intrusions.

[43] It
is obvious that non party witnesses are burdened by being obliged to appear and
to answer the questions put to them. If they need to produce documents, and for
that purpose search for same, the process can be fastidious. However, the
process of justice exacts such a price. As have often been said, it is not the
best system possible but it is the best system we have to arrive at a fair and
complete resolution of the litigation.  The Court does its best not to impose
an undue burden on those who are called to appear before it.
[63]

[
112
]

Absent agreement, no fees should be recoverable for internal work
required by a witness to locate responsive documents or prepare for the
examination. The court can require that reasonable costs be paid for any
third-party fees actually incurred and paid in duplicating a copy for the
purpose of communicating that copy.
[64]

4.

DISCRETION AND CRITERIA APPLIED TO THE
APPLICATION

[
113
]

The Court now turns to the Application and the Document Demands.

4.1

Hearing in the U.S. which lead to Request

[
114
]

Rossetti and Canam Group disputed the nature of the hearing in the
U.S. Litigation which led to the Request.

[
115
]

As part of the procedural differences raised by Canam Group, the
parties in the U.S. Litigation file notice pleadings. For the purpose of the
hearing in the U.S. Litigation on Rossetti’s request to issue letters rogatory,
the parties also provided written submissions, notably  Rossetti’s June 3, 2020
and Canam Steel’s June 8, 2020 letters,  filed respectively as Exhibit R-3 and
Exhibit R-4 in support of the Application. Rossetti and Canam Group each
accepted that the record in the U.S. Litigation for the hearing included not
only the notice pleadings but also those letters.

[
116
]

Canam Group argued that the Court owed little deference to the
determinations made by the U.S. court on relevance.  It argued that the hearing
in the U.S. Litigation involved only a summary hearing on sparse documents and
involve only a brief phone call prior to the Request being issued.

[
117
]

Rossetti disagreed with that characterization of the level of
attention given to its request.  It filed a copy of the docket for the U.S.
Litigation and its Application included Rossetti’s and Canam Steel’s letter
submissions.

[
118
]

Canam Group also questioned whether a list with the equivalent text
comprising each of the Document Demands was submitted for the hearing in the
U.S Litigation. The Court notes that Canam Steel’s own June 8, 2020 letter
refers to specific document categories by number and subjects which correspond
to the same numbering and subjects as those before the Court on the
Application.  The docket filed by Rossetti also includes reference to the
filing of the list of document demands.

[
119
]

The Court will return to this issue and the role of deference when
addressing relevance later in the decision.

4.2

Initial Scope

[
120
]

The Request contains a statement of the scope of the subject matter
(“
Initial Scope
”).

The
documents and testimony of a corporate representative sought by Rossetti from
Canam Group by issuance of these Letters Rogatory fall into two discrete
categories. (1) Documents and testimony related to
the allegations
that
Canam Group conducted an internal assessment and decided to restructure its
heavy structural steel division and cease bidding on similar large scale
projects after a number of high profile project failures, including, but not
limited to, the project at issue in this action, which is the Arthur Ashe
Tennis Stadium located in Flushing Meadows, New York; and (2) Documents and
testimony related to the manufacturing capacity of Canam Group’s St. Gedeon de
Beauce plant both before and after the reorganization.

[
121
]

Drawing from the Initial Scope, Rossetti’s submitted the following
statement of the subject matter in its draft judgment on its Application:

ORDERS
that the examination shall cover only the following subject matter and issues:

(a) The
question of whether Canam Group conducted an internal assessment and decided to
restructure its heavy structural steel division and ceased bidding on large
scale projects after a number of high profile project failures, including, but
not limited to, the project at issue in the above US Court case, which is the
Arthur Ashe Tennis Stadium located in Flushing Meadows, New York and the
reasons why;

(b) The
question of manufacturing capacity of steel of Canam Group’s St. Gedéon de
Beauce plant during the years 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2017;

[
122
]

Both the Initial Scope and the Document Demands issued from the U.S.
Litigation.  Rossetti’s Québec counsel did not draft either but were tasked

6.1

Relevance

[
158
]

Presented with an application to authorize execution of a rogatory
commission, a Québec court has two (2) standards of relevance to consider.

[
159
]

First, the requested evidence must be relevant for the purpose of
the foreign dispute resolution according to the foreign court’s own standard of
relevance.  If the evidence does not meet the foreign court’s standards, then
the Québec court need not authorize execution of a rogatory commission to
collect it.  The hearing on whether to authorize the process ends there.

[
160
]

In this respect, the Québec court owes deference to the foreign
court’s initial determination of relevance.  Deference acknowledges that a
presumption exists that the foreign court’s determination is valid.  The
presumption is rebuttable. Evidence regarding the nature of the hearing and the
submissions may rebut that presumption.  With sufficient insight into the
hearing conducted in the foreign court, the Québec court can determine whether
it disagrees in whole or in part with that determination.

[
161
]

Second, the standard of relevance in the foreign court and its
determination do not bind the Québec court. Rather, if the foreign court’s
determination of relevance remains valid, the Québec court will then determine whether,
according to Québec standards of relevance, the evidence sought from the witness
located here is relevant. Deference does not eliminate discretion.

[
162
]

A Québec court will not order communication of more evidence that what
Québec standards also determine are relevant. If the evidence meets Québec
standards, then the court can order that the witness participate in the oral
and documentary pre-trial phase to assist the foreign court, provided the other
criteria are also met.

York

163
]

action.  Relevance is a matter of degree, and the standard is applied more
liberally in discovery than it is at trial

claims and do look to other elements, including the exhibits communicated, to
determine relevance.
[77]

[
174
]

At the stage of authorizing execution of the rogatory commission, a
Québec court does not decide the strength of any position taken on an issue in
regard to which the evidence is held to be relevant.  Determining relevance
does not require that the court first or also determine whether the position
taken is well-founded.  Relevance is determined independent of the requesting
party’s chances of success when adducing the evidence, in whole or in part.

Applying Québec
relevance to the U.S. Litigation

[
175
]

Canam Group rightly argued that Québec civil procedure differs in
some important manners from other common law jurisdictions in Canada.
[78]
The Court adds, as noted
above, that similar distinctions also exist with the U.S. and the nature of the
pleadings. As appears from the case law filed by
Rossetti and Canam Group, Québec courts refer to and follow the reasoning in
Ontario decisions. The Court notes that courts in Ontario consider evidence
relevant if it has a tendency, as a matter of logic, common sense and human
experience, to help resolve an issue at trial.
[79]

[
176
]

As noted earlier, the parties submitted letters June 3, 2020 and
June 8, 2020 which expand on the summary allegations in the notice style
pleadings set out in Complaint and the Answer. In its submissions to the Court
on the Application, Canam Group expressly likened both those letters to interim
procedures and motions.

[
177
]

Based on the record and guided by
Glegg
,
Fuoco
and
Dominion
Nickel
, the Court determines that it can rely on the June 3, 2020 and June
8, 2020 letters for the purpose of determining relevance as they form part of

relevance. The letters complete the understanding of the summary style notice
pleadings and Canam Steel’s own submissions acknowledge that the claims arise

6.2

Representative of Canam Group to attend as witness

[
178
]

A rogatory commission seeks a source of evidence. The source can be
an individual or an entity, such as a corporation, partnership or association.
That source is identified as the witness in the rogatory commission. When the
source is an individual, the witness and the source are the same.  When the
source is a corporation, the witness and the source are distinct. In the
latter, the source identifies its representative to serve as the witness. In
either event, a rogatory commission requests that the source - the individual
or a representative of a specific entity - attend to give oral testimony and
communicate documents.  The source becomes the named responding party to the
application in the Québec Superior Court for the execution of the rogatory
commission.  As a party to that application, the source – either the individual
or the entity - has standing and opportunity to respond before being ordered to
participate.

[
179
]

The evidence sought in the foreign court might involve eyewitness
testimony to a motor vehicle accident, participation in negotiations or
involvement in contract performance.  The evidence might also involve reliable
information related to a commercial dispute and held by a corporate non-party.

[
180
]

The Request seeks evidence from Canam Group.  Canam Group can only
testify through a representative, as acknowledged in the Request.  The
Application specifies the identity of the individual sought to serve as the witness.

[
181
]

The courts must be mindful that, when imposing an obligation to
provide testimony and communicate documents, they must not inadvertently put
the witness at risk of disclosing information which would breach the witness’
obligations. Ordering a witness to disclose personal information capable of
identifying employees may breach that witness’ obligations under applicable
privacy legislation.  Though the information may be relevant, the court ought
not to be order it to be communicated without considering the obligations which
may prevent communication, in whole or in part, here and outside the
jurisdiction. Agreement by the corporate entity to communicate the information
is not necessarily a complete answer to the witness’ obligations.

[
182
]

For pre-trial examinations in Canada, the process to select the representative
for an entity can vary from jurisdiction.

[
183
]

In some jurisdictions, the practice is that the party requesting the
examination selects the individual to be examined and the individual must have
personal knowledge of the facts on which he or she testifies.  The freedom to
select, even against the choice of the other party, comes with having to accept
the limits of the evidence chosen.  If the examining party insisted on the
wrong witness, then it requires consent to examine a second representative or
authorization of the court.  In such cases, the party examining and the party
being examined share an interest in agreeing on the identity of the witness.

[
184
]

In other jurisdictions, the party being examined chooses the witness
and that witness need not have personal knowledge of the facts, having the
obligation to inform himself or herself of the facts prior to attending.
[80]

[
185
]

Québec courts must be alert to these variations when considering the
identity of the representative who will serve as witness. The courts ought to
consider if the parties from different jurisdictions agree on who chooses the
representative and whether the chosen representative must have personal
knowledge or merely the obligation to inform oneself.

[
186
]

Without prejudice to their submissions on the merits of the
Application, Rossetti and Canam Group informed the Court that they had agreed
that Mr. Marc Dutil could attend as the representative for Canam Group.  Canam
Group, through its counsel, confirmed that Mr. Dutil had agreed to attend in
that capacity and attend on January 14, 2022, the date set by Rossetti, Canam
Group, the Other U.S. Defendants and Canam Steel.

[
187
]

Rossetti submitted a draft order which, among other things, included
the mention of Mr. Dutil as the representative as well as an order against Mr.
Dutil personally requiring him to participate in the oral examination and
document communication.  Canam Group agreed to that wording.

[
188
]

Despite the agreement and despite case law which likens authorization
to issuing a subpoena, the Court will not issue an order directly against Mr.
Dutil.  He did not personally appear before the Court and is not the actual
source sought in the Request.  The Court will order the attendance of a Canam
Group representative.  The Court will limit mention of Mr. Dutil to taking act
of the confirmation of Mr. Dutil’s willingness to participate.  The core of the
Request is not the identity of a particular individual serving as Canam Group’s
representative but evidence held by Canam Group. The Court will therefore
provide that the identity of the Canam Group representative can be changed by
Rossetti and Canam Group.

[

Group’s arguments had been effectively heard already in the U.S. Litigation
and, despite them, the Request had issued. Deference for the prior

]

and annual report.  It argued that the interpretation was unsupported, irrelevant

contested being drawn into the U.S. Litigation, arguing that it was a non-party

[
192
]

Elements of Canam Group’s arguments do appear in the record in the

the business decisions of a public company in Canada
” to Hunt’s

Referring to its own history of “
fabricating steel for large stadium

Steel

”.  Canam Steel’s responses
redirected the focus back onto the dispute between Rossetti and Canam Steel.

[

]

With regard to whether the evidence is not otherwise obtainable,
Canam Steel asserted that it had already produced relevant documents which do “
test
the veracity of Canam [Steel]’s bid on the Project
” and that the relevant
documents had been communicated regarding Canam Steel’s “
bidding history and
practices for this Project and others
”.

[
194
]

The U.S. Litigation involves a dispute between sophisticated parties
who chose to contract with specific parties for the Project. Rossetti
alleges no facts susceptible of justifying application of
article 317
of the

Civil Code of Québec, CQLR c CCQ-1991
(“
C.C.Q.

or Canam Group.

]

determination on those submissions and the Request appears to reproduce
Rossetti’s position.

[
196
]

Use of “
Canam
” as a component of trade names serves to
brand the structure but not to renounce to the separations between its many
corporate entities. Overlapping use of “
Canam

more allegations, cannot override the fundamental principle in Québec civil law
that corporate persons have distinct legal personalities and patrimonies.
[81]
Independent of trade names,
Canam Group’s mere position as parent situated atop the corporate structure
does not, absent more allegations, extinguish its separate status. Canam Group
may venture into the worldwide economy but does so through distinct corporate
entities.

[

]

The Court does not suggest that, in other types of disputes, a
parent company can always maintain its distance.  A foreign court dispute might
involve an extracontractual (tort) cause of action or allegations of ostensible
authority of a subsidiary due to the parent’s own conduct. In such instances, a
Québec court might be prompted to examine whether the parent is a genuine
stranger to the dispute in the foreign court.  Such is not the case raised in
the U.S. Litigation.

]

]

[
204
]

Rossetti justifies its request to obtain evidence from Rossetti,
arguing that its Application is narrowed by two (2) factors: the evidence is

and, the evidence is (i)
“limited to a (sic) narrow and discrete issues,
namely the reorganization of Canam’s Heavy Structural Steel division, which
undeniable (sic) resulted from its failure to properly estimate projects”
.
Canam Group resists both these points. It argues that, unless the scope is
limited to relevant documents and relevant testimony, the Application
essentially puts Canam Group’s operations on trial.

[

]

Regarding Rossetti’s first factor, the Court reminds that the U.S.
Litigation involves a dispute between Canam Steel and Rossetti, along with
others involved in construction of the Arthur Ashe Tennis Stadium.  Rossetti’s
reliance on the size of the claim made against it by Canam Steel cannot
justify, without more, examination of a non-party’s operations.

[

Regarding Rossetti’s second factor, the Court notes that Rossetti’s submissions
combine two (2) elements: reorganization of the heavy structural steel division
and failure to properly estimate projects.  The record presented for the
Application discloses that Canam Group undertook the reorganization whereas Canam
Steel is alleged to have failed to properly bid on the contract.  Rossetti may
conflate the reorganization and bid failure but the record in the U.S. Litigation

[82]
in the U.S. Litigation,

in the bidding process and does so in the context of its defence against Canam

may include heavy structural steel activities. The dispute between Rossetti and
Canam Steel in the U.S. Litigation may well require the N.Y. Court to consider

limited to
“whether Canam [Steel]’s own internal systematic failures, and not
any alleged representations [by Rossetti], caused it to underbid the Project
”.
