In Québec, documents provided in the context of the pre-trial
discovery process are subject to the implicit undertaking of confidentiality
confirmed by
Lac d'Amiante
. Part of that undertaking involves
restraining use of the information to the dispute resolution process in which
it was obtained. The parties receiving the information cannot use it for other
purposes, including additional dispute resolution. That aspect of the undertaking
continues to apply, during and after the hearing on the merits.

[
230
]

The Québec court in which the dispute resolution proceeded, and no
other court, retains the exclusive jurisdiction in first instance to relieve
the parties and their counsel of the implicit obligation of confidentiality governing
information communicated in that court’s pre-trial process.  The Court of
Québec and the Québec Superior Court each retain their respective exclusive
jurisdiction to authorize a receiving party to repurpose the evidence communicated
in the pre-trial discovery process before them.

[
231
]

As noted, a rogatory commission can address pre-trial evidence and
not just for trials.  Because the Québec Superior Court authorizes the
communication of such evidence for pre-trial when it authorizes the execution
of a rogatory commission, the Superior Court has exclusive jurisdiction to release
receiving parties of their obligation not to repurpose the information
received.

[
232
]

Québec courts are mindful that certain protections, common here, do
not automatically arise elsewhere.  Québec courts are equally mindful that
other protections, available upon motion to the court, might not be available
from a foreign court.  Québec courts also acknowledge that parties to the
foreign court litigation are not bound by the Québec courts’ orders unless
those parties were a party to the application.

[
233
]

Rossetti and Canam Group have confirmed that the Other U.S.
Defendants and Canam Steel will access the evidence resulting from execution of
the rogatory commission authorized by the Court. The Other U.S. Defendants and
Canam Steel are not parties to the adjudication of the Application in the
present matter but will have access to the testimony and the documents
communicated. The Court has no jurisdiction over the Other U.S. Defendants and
Canam Steel and none have indicated that they have attorned in whole or in
part.

[
234
]

The Court wishes to authorize the full participation of the Other
U.S. Defendants and Canam Steel in the rogatory commission initiated by
Rossetti for the purpose of the U.S. Litigation but without compromising the
implied undertaking and Canam Group’s rights.

[
235
]

The Court has discretion to require that a foreign court impose terms
and conditions regarding access to such evidence before the parties gain access
to the evidence. Doing so satisfies comity but not at the expense of the
witness.

[
236
]

The Court recognizes that the Other U.S. Defendants and Canam Steel
can then file the evidence in the U.S. court record.  The latter is not a part
of the implied undertaking of confidentiality.  That said, the Court can
consider imposing terms and conditions on that filing if doing so is justified
for the criteria.

[
237
]

In addition to the implied undertaking, the Court will require, as a
condition precedent to access, that the U.S. court issue an order which extends
protections which exist in Québec and govern the communication of evidence. Doing
so will encourage non-parties to provide fuller communication of relevant
testimony and documents deemed relevant to the conduct of the dispute
resolution in the U.S. Litigation.

8.2

Solicitor-client documents – Binder C

[
238
]

The parties disputed access to documents over which Canam Group
claimed solicitor-client privilege. The parties did not dispute the applicable
principles.

[
239
]

Solicitor-client privilege stems not just from legislation
[89]
but also recognition by the
courts. Privilege arises when information involves: (i) a communication between
solicitor and client; (ii) which entails the seeking or giving of legal advice;
and (iii) which is intended to be confidential by the parties.
[90]
The privilege applies to the
contents and not its form, thereby encompassing a variety of documents and activity
by in-house counsel.
[91]

The Court will use the terms solicitor, counsel and attorney when discussing
solicitor-client privilege.

[
240
]

Solicitor-client privilege applies as long as the communication falls
within “
the usual and ordinary scope
” of the attorney’s relationship
and, once established, is “considerably broad and all-encompassing”.
[92]
The Court notes that art.
2858 C.C.Q. provides that the courts, even on their own motion, must reject any
evidence obtained as a result of a breach of professional privilege.

[
241
]

Not all facts and events with which attorneys deal with in the
execution of their mandates are covered by professional secrecy, nor does the
legal institution of professional secrecy exempt attorneys from testifying
about facts involving their clients in all situations.
[93]

[
242
]

As is custom in such matters, the privileged documents in Binder C were
communicated to the Court, without copy to Rossetti, to conduct a
voir dire
.
To make a decision as to whether the privilege attaches, the documents must be
read by the court, which requires, at a minimum, that the documents be under
the jurisdiction of a court.
[94]

The Court examined each of the documents provided by Canam Group in Binder C. Canam
Group also provided evidence regarding the status of attorney and role as
attorney for certain individuals involved in the exchanges contained in Binder C

[
243
]

In light of the applicable elements noted above to establish the solicitor-client
privilege, the Court determines that the exchanges set out in the documents
included in Binder C qualify for the solicitor-client privilege invoked by
Canam Group.  To preserve the privilege invoked, the Court refrains from
setting out the contents of the exchanges. The Court maintains Canam Group’s
objections in regard to the documents in Binder C.

8.3

Litigation privilege documents – Binder B

[
244
]

The parties disputed access to documents over which Canam Group
claimed litigation privilege.  Again, the parties did not dispute the
applicable principles.

[
245
]

Litigation privilege attaches to documents created for the dominant
purpose of litigation and, being neither absolute nor permanent, expires when
the dispute resolution for which it was created ends.
[95]
Once the document holder
establishes that the document was created for the dominant purpose of
litigation and the litigation in question or related litigation is pending or
may reasonably be apprehended, a
prima facie
rebuttable presumption of
inadmissibility arises.
[96]

[
246
]

Litigation privilege is viewed as a limited exception to the
principle of full disclosure, offering a narrower protection and different
rationale than solicitor-client privilege.
[97]

Litigation privilege and solicitor-client privilege serve a common cause but differ
conceptually. Litigation privilege ensures the efficacy of the adversarial
process whereas solicitor-client privilege protects the relationship.
[98]
Litigation privilege ensures
that parties enjoy privacy in the preparation of their positions for dispute
resolution whereas solicitor-client privilege ensures that parties can access
professional advice required to engage in dispute resolution.
[99]

[
247
]

Litigation privilege does not target only solicitor-client
communications.  It applies also to unrepresented parties and non-confidential
documents.
[100]

It can be likened to settlement privilege
[101]

and, like mediation discussions, serves an important purpose.  Litigation
privilege can be asserted against third parties.
[102]
Allowing access to others
would undermine fundamental principles necessary to dispute resolution.
[103]
Canada’s Supreme Court
endorsed the reasoning of the U.S. Supreme Court when confirming that it would
be inappropriate to exclude third parties from the application of the
privilege.
[104]

[
248
]

There is nothing to suggest that the term “
litigation
” excludes
non-court dispute resolution before arbitration proceedings, both statutory and
consensual, and administrative tribunals.  Use of the term “
litigation
” ought
not to eliminate such other forms of dispute resolution.  Those forms
necessarily form part of the adversarial process which the privilege exists to
protect.  The distinction need not be explored in the present case to decide
the objection. On the present record, the documents in Binder B meet the
standard as stated and the contents demonstrate that they were created for the
dominant purpose of litigation.

[
249
]

As with the preceding set of documents over which Canam Group
claimed solicitor-client privilege, the documents subject to litigation
privilege were communicated in Binder B to the Court, without copy to Rossetti,
to conduct a
voir dire
. The Court examined each of the documents in
Binder B with the applicable principles in mind, and with the information,
provided by Canam Group, about the relative status and role of certain
individuals involved in the exchanges.

[
250
]

In light of the applicable elements noted above to establish litigation
privilege, the Court determines that the exchanges set out in the documents
included in Binder B qualify for the litigation privilege invoked by Canam
Group.  Their dominant purpose appears from the face of the documents and
appear to be active disputes. To preserve the privilege invoked, the Court
refrains from setting out the contents of the exchanges. The Court maintains
Canam Group’s objections in regard to the documents in Binder B.

8.4

Confidential documents - Binders D and E

[
251
]

The parties disputed access to documents over which Canam Group
claimed they qualified for protection of its legitimate interests.  Again, the parties
did not dispute the applicable principles.

[
252
]

Sierra Club of Canada v. Canada (Minister of Finance),
2002 SCC 41
(CanLII)
,
[2002] 2 SCR 522
(“
Sierra Club
”) identified
two (2) branches of the test for issuing confidentiality orders concerning
documents filed in the court record. A confidentiality order should only be
granted when (i) necessary to prevent a serious risk to an important interest,
including a commercial interest, in the context of litigation because
reasonably alternative measures will not prevent the risk; and (ii) the beneficial
effects of the confidentiality order, including the effects on the right of the
parties to a fair process, outweigh its harmful effects.
[105]

[
253
]

The first branch includes three (3) important. First, the risk must
be real and substantial, well grounded in evidence, posing a serious threat to
the commercial interest in question.  Second, the important commercial interest
must be one which can be expressed in terms of a public interest in
confidentiality, where there is a general principle at stake.  Third, the court
is required to consider whether reasonable alternatives are available to such
an order how to restrict the order as much as is reasonably possible while
preserving the commercial interest in question.

[
254
]

The Supreme Court noted that the information must have been treated
as confidential at all relevant times and that commercial interests could
reasonably be harmed by disclosure of the information provided that the
information had been held with a reasonable expectation of it being kept
confidential.

[
255
]

The Québec Court of Appeal remains vigilant on protecting the open
court principle and regularly endorses dismissals of confidentiality orders
issued in first instance which fail to comply with the test required.
[106]
The Court notes that the
analysis which precedes issuance of such orders presumes that (i) the implied
undertaking of confidentiality already serves much of the purpose sought by
proposed confidentiality orders
[107]

and (ii) other measures are available in the civil litigation process.
[108]

[
256
]

In the present case, the Court is asked to order a non-party located
in Québec to communicate sensitive financial information to others, including
market competitors, located in another country for their use.  The Court is
asked to do so according to the
Sierra Club
line of cases but (i) without
limitations inherent in the litigation process here and (ii) without any
opportunity to issue measures to protect the information, if and when filed, in
whole or in part, in the public record in the foreign country. The non-party
has no subsequent standing in the foreign litigation to seek and obtain
adequate protection which may be inherent in the options offered in civil
litigation in Québec.
[109]

[
257
]

The Court identifies a public interest eligible for the test in
Sierra
Club
.  In response to comity, the courts can provide meaningful assistance
when requested and, as required by the case law, do so without prejudice to
sovereignty and the rights of the witness providing the sensitive information. That
test is set by
Zingre
and remains valid today.  The public interest is
served when the Court orders a non-party to comply with a request from a
foreign court while imposing conditions which are no more onerous than those which
arise automatically by the nature of the civil litigation here and available
upon application from the courts.
[110]

[
258
]

Judicial policy justified recognition of the implicit undertaking of
confidentiality as a core principle applicable to ordering witnesses to
communicate sensitive information.  If the purpose of comity is to provide
assistance, then the Court is authorized to offer the same range of incentives
which animate the discovery process here.

[74]
There are other judicial policy reasons why it is legitimate to recognize the
confidentiality rule.  As we have seen, examination on discovery is an
exploratory proceeding. As Fish J.A. pointed out in his reasons, the purpose of
the examination is to encourage the most complete disclosure of the information
available, despite the privacy imperative.  On the other hand, if a party is
afraid that information will be made public as a result of an examination, that
may be a disincentive to disclose documents or answer certain questions candidly,
which would be contrary to the proper administration of justice and the
objective of full disclosure of the evidence. Recognizing the implied
obligation of confidentiality will reduce that risk, by protecting the party
concerned against disclosure of information that would otherwise not have been
used in the case in which the examination was held and the information was
disclosed.
[111]

[
259
]

As noted earlier, the Court’s discretion to execute the rogatory
commission involves consideration of three (3) elements: comity, public policy
of the jurisdiction to which the request is directed, and absence of prejudice
to the sovereignty or the witnesses of that jurisdiction.
[112]
The Court can ensure that
its execution of the rogatory commission does not (i) violate relevant Canadian
or provincial law; (ii) infringe on recognized Canadian moral or legal
principles; (iii) impose an undue burden on the witness of whom the request is
made; or (iv) do prejudice to that witness.
[113]

[
260
]

In the public interest of responding meaningfully to letters
rogatory as a matter of comity and compliant with respect for public policy
related to the implicit undertaking and to avoid prejudice to the witness, the
Court can impose conditions on the communication of the information in order to
replicate the protections (i) inherent in the pre-trial discovery process and
(ii) available in the course of civil litigation, subject to applicable
measures.

[
261
]

The order would respect the rights of a non-party to preserve the
existing confidentiality of sensitive commercial documents and allow the parties
in the U.S. Litigation to advance in the trial. The intrusion would be minimal,
and others would not be significantly affected by not accessing entirety of the
still-current information.

[
262
]

A confidentiality order would have significant beneficial effects on
the U.S. Litigation and reduce risk to Canam Group suffering a risk of harm to
its competitive position.  Without a confidentiality order, Canam Group might withhold
the documents in order to protect its commercial interests but still relevant
to Rossetti’s defence in the U.S. Litigation. Rossetti’s inability to adduce
that evidence in the U.S. Litigation would hinder its right to make full answer
and defence.

[
263
]

Though important, the protection for confidential documents is
interpreted and applied restrictively.
[114]

The protection applies, among other things, to financial information regarded
as sensitive and especially when the recipients are competitors.
[115]
Rossetti’s Application would
oblige a non-party to share sensitive financial information with other market
players and which might give others unasked for advantages.

[
264
]

Rossetti argued that the information sought covers a period which should
qualify the information as stale.  It relies on
Distributions d'acier de
Montréal v. Tubes Olympia ltée,
2016 QCCS 1635
which observed that the
information dating back three (3) to five (5) years would not prejudice a
party’s operations.  In that case, the plaintiff resisted communication of
financial information despite having itself alleged in its proceedings that it
filed a notice under the
Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, RSC 1985, c B-3
and
having communicated a copy of its notice of intention as an exhibit in support
of its claim. The court correctly held that a fair debate under
articles 17
and

20

C.C.P.
required communication information alleged by one party against
another party.
[116]

The Court agrees with the finding.

[
265
]

The Court determines that, on the present record, the  Document Demands
target sensitive information applicable to a period in which the information
remains current to the non-party’s operations and merits protection.  As
already stated, Canam Group’s operations are not on trial and, as such,
financial information regarding the operations are not, without more, relevant
or at the heart of the U.S. Litigation and can be separated from communication.
[117]

[
266
]

The Court also observes that the Other U.S. Defendants appear to be
significant market participants involved in large scale projects and ought not
to be given access to information which could create the appearance of a
competitive advantage.  None of the Other U.S. Defendants seek an unnecessary
advantage and the Court must not authorize communication of information which (i)
overreaches the purpose needed in the U.S. Litigation and (ii) permits the
appearance of allowing access to information which can be commercially sensitive.

[
267
]

Canam Group did not put its financial information in question and as
a non-party to the U.S. Litigation has not formal status to require a
reciprocity even if it wanted to have it.  Canam Group has demonstrated that it
has procedures to keep such information confidential and has not renounced to
it by its conduct in the litigation.
[118]

Its willingness to argue in defense of access to its documents does not qualify
as waiver or render anything about the information public
per se
.
[119]
The Court also does not
know the extent to which the documents, once filed in the court record in the
U.S. can be retrieved and, if so, under which circumstances.
[120]

[
268
]

The Court notes that the relevance of such information is not about
the amounts and identify of different projects but the process of decision
making and reasoning.  That process relates to Canam Group conducting an internal
assessment, deciding to restructure its heavy structural steel division and/or ceasing
bidding on large scale projects during one (1) or more of the years 2013, 2014,
2015, 2016 and 2017 for bids and projects involving Canam Steel Corporation and
its reasons, if any, why it did so conduct, decide and/or cease.

[
269
]

The Court examined each of the documents communicated in Binders D
and E and can acknowledge that in a handful of instances, the redactions fill
more of the document that the information left.  That said, the type of
document and remaining information even in those documents can provide some
assistance.  The other documents, even redacted, provide substantial
information for use in the U.S. Litigation. The Court can allow access to
redacted documents and, in doing so, assist in the fact-finding process sought
for the U.S. Litigation but without prejudice to the non-party.

[
270
]

In light of the applicable principles noted above to establish a
confidentiality interest and justify protection, the Court determines that the
exchanges set out in the documents included in Binders D and E qualify for the confidentiality
interest invoked by Canam Group.  The sensitivity of the information appears
from the face of the documents and appears to be current information of ongoing
importance to Canam Group.  The information was and remains protected by an
existing code in force and respected by Canam Group. To preserve the  confidentiality
interest invoked, the Court will maintain Canam Group’s objection in part, and order
that the documents in Binders D and E over which Canam Group asserts confidentiality
be communicated but in redacted form.

[
271
]

The communication also benefits from the orders regarding implied
undertaking of confidentiality and confidentiality to be included as
preconditions to communication.

9.

CONDUCT OF ROGATORY COMMISSION

[
272
]

The draft submitted to the Court contained the necessary details

[
274

The Court also observed the Request that the witness’ “
examination
be filmed such that a video recording may be produced
” and that, “
a
court reporter and videographer be permitted to attend the requested oral

275

[
276
]

The Request further sought to have the order stipulate that the
examination be taken pursuant to the U.S.
Federal Rules of Civil Procedure

and
Federal Rules of Evidence
“
[e]xcept to the extent that such rules
are incompatible with the rules of the Province of Quebec
”.

[
277
]

Rossetti adduced excerpts of those rules and Canam Group did not

[
278
]

Rossetti asked that the Court authorize non-members of the Québec
bar to attend the examination and conduct the questioning.  Canam Group agreed
with the approach but asked that the representative attending as witness and Canam
Group be allowed to have counsel present for the limited purpose of attending
for the witness.  Canam Group did not submit that it would need different

attendance to attend as counsel to a witness, understanding that it is a
limited role.

10.

COSTS

[
279
]

Regarding the taxable judicial costs of the Application, the Court
observes that they are nominal and, in the circumstances, ought not to be

Rossetti and Canam Group provided transparent and fulsome responses to all
